entries.title: The Coming Food-Stamp Crisis
entries.summary: A looming deadline may force some states to end SNAP next year.
entries.content:
A looming deadline may force some states to end SNAP next year.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Back in April, Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, wrote an op-ed celebrating the Trump administration’s efforts to get Americans off food stamps. Officially known as SNAP, the program has shed an estimated 6 million participants since Donald Trump’s return to office—a shift that Rollins argued could help break a “vicious cycle” of government dependence.

The idea that too many people have come to rely on federal handouts has long been a line of attack against SNAP. Per the Department of Agriculture’s preliminary data from April, about 37 million low- and no-income people in the United States are on food stamps. That’s roughly one in 10 Americans, down from one in eight last year. The reduction is in line with the administration’s broader approach to social welfare. Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump has touted as one of his signature policy achievements, slashed funding to Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. And its cuts to SNAP—tightening eligibility requirements and limiting the amount of aid that recipients might be able to collect in the future—were the largest in the program’s history.

Food stamps will lose $186 billion in federal funding through 2034, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s estimates. But what Rollins has framed as a way to curtail waste, fraud, and abuse is already having far-reaching impacts on the Americans who rely on the program. Last week, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank, suggested that “it’s very likely that the number of children receiving SNAP has dropped by more than 1.5 million since July 2025,” when the OBBBA became law. Inflation has been rising quickly this year, in part because of the Iran war, and the assault on food stamps is now compounding an ongoing affordability crisis. If states can’t meet the federal government’s new requirements for SNAP, they may have to take on a collective $9 billion in food-stamp costs themselves—forcing local legislators to make hard choices about which kinds of social-welfare programs, and which kinds of people, should receive aid.

This past winter, when the White House decided to briefly stop funding SNAP during the government shutdown, Trump said that the program’s enrollment number was “many times what it should be.” It’s true that food-stamp enrollment—which tends to rise during moments of economic crisis and contract in moments of recovery—spiked substantially during the coronavirus pandemic as Congress temporarily increased benefit amounts, and enrollment still hasn’t reverted to its pre-2020 level. But stricter work requirements (homeless people and veterans are no longer exempt, for example) and reductions in federal funding have helped drive down SNAP enrollment at a vertiginous moment. Most people, whether on food stamps or not, are cutting back on groceries. And no other institution “is going to swoop in and provide these financial resources” to families struggling to buy groceries, Lauren Bauer, a fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, told me.

In Arizona, the number of people with access to SNAP benefits has almost halved in less than a year—the biggest drop in any state. A recent New York Times report explains that the OBBBA’s cuts and updated rules have created “bureaucratic chaos” in the state, which has been exacerbated by a labyrinthian paperwork process and antiquated tech infrastructure. The fact that Arizona laid off a third of its caseworkers after losing a federal grant has also made it harder to verify who is and isn’t eligible for aid—and monthly visits to food banks have outpaced SNAP enrollment in the state for the first time, according to the Times.

States have historically managed SNAP payments on their own; the federal government supplies the money for benefits and for some of the administrative costs. Critics of this arrangement have noted that the post-COVID swell in enrollments has coincided with an uptick in improper payments, most of which have historically been overpayments. In 2019, 7.4 percent of the payments SNAP doled out were made in error, according to the USDA; last year, the national error rate was 10.6 percent. The OBBBA puts states in a tough spot. When it went into effect, it gave most states until the end of September 2026 to get their error rates below 6 percent—a little more than a year. If they fail to do so, they will begin sharing the cost of food-stamp benefits with the White House in 2027 (Alaska and other states with higher error rates will have longer deadlines).

The consequences will affect red and blue states alike, unlike some other Trump-backed economic initiatives. According to data released by the USDA last month, 41 states had error rates above the threshold in the 2025 fiscal year, and many are now scrambling to get those numbers down. California could end up paying roughly $1.9 billion if legislators don’t find a way to reduce the state’s rate by almost half, and Florida may need to pay $900 million, according to one estimate. Taking on those costs would require states to radically reshape their budgets, raise taxes, or find some other way to pay for SNAP—otherwise, their constituents may hold them accountable when the food-stamp payments stop coming. Officials in Alabama and Arizona have already considered ending the program, and, in an anonymous survey, four states identified “withdrawing and/or pausing from SNAP” as a potential risk.

If states are able to lower their error rates, SNAP could be transformed for the better. But if they fail to do so by the fast-approaching deadline, it’s hard to see who wins: not food-stamp recipients, not the states that will have their budgets upended, and not the administration, which has been trying to convince Americans ahead of the midterms that it’s responding to their affordability concerns. Rollins has described SNAP as a “broken program,” but these changes aren’t guaranteed to restore trust in the system. Instead, the push to repair SNAP could end up breaking it even more.

Here are four new stories from The Atlantic:

Today’s News

  • President Trump threatened to temporarily withdraw Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney generaluntil Republican Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who are holdouts, leave office in January.
  • Iran and the United States continued exchanging missile strikes today; drone strikes targeted Egypt for the first time.
  • FIFA proposed spinning off the commercial rights of its major tournaments into a private company and then selling a 20 percent stake of it to investors. UEFA member nations argued that the plan would give private investors too much influence over soccer and threatened to boycott all FIFA competitionsif the $20 billion deal goes through.

Dispatches

  • Time-Travel Thursdays: Since the 19th century, office jobs have represented a path to comfort and prestige, Jake Lundberg writes. The AI era istesting whether that promise still holds.

Explore all of our newsletters here.

Evening Read

The Cities That Said Yes to Drugs

By Michael Powell

Late last year, I walked roughly a mile from downtown Seattle to the working-class neighborhood of Little Saigon and came upon a montage of human despair. An open-air drug market stretched along the intersection of 12th and Jackson: about 250 people, many smoking fentanyl or bent over in the thrall of the drug, tilting as if mid-fall. Three women lay passed out on the sidewalk, their chests slowly rising and falling, while fellow addicts stepped over them and dealers made sales. Young boys, schoolbags on their backs, stood on a far corner and watched …

Seattle, like a striking number of other liberal American cities, has embraced a radical form of “harm reduction,” which is more a philosophy about treating addiction than a scientific approach to it.

entries.title: Zelensky Asked Trump for a Favor From Elon Musk
entries.summary: Ukraine wants to start using Musk’s Starlink to target ballistic-missile launchers inside Russia.
entries.content:
Ukraine wants to start using Musk’s Starlink to target ballistic-missile launchers inside Russia.

During closed-door talks at the White House on Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky laid out a plan for his country to survive another winter of war with Russia. For it to work, President Trump would need to call in a big favor from his ally Elon Musk. But according to two officials familiar with the conversation, Trump was noncommittal, leaving the future of the plan in doubt.

The new proposal, which has not been previously reported, offered the United States a way around sending Ukraine advanced air-defense missiles, known as Patriot interceptors, which the war in Iran has dramatically depleted. Instead, Ukraine would expand its use of another American technology: the Starlink satellite-communications network, which Musk controls.

Zelensky asked Trump to secure Musk’s permission for the use of Starlink to guide drone strikes inside Russia, according to the two officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. (A third official confirmed Zelensky’s request.) Up to now, Musk has allowed the Ukrainians to use Starlink only on their own territory, including in Crimea and other regions that Russia has occupied. Musk’s aerospace company, SpaceX, has restricted the use of Starlink inside Russia.

Ukraine’s campaign of long-range drone strikes has therefore employed less reliable targeting methods, including onboard computers with AI-powered navigation tools. These weapons have been effective at hitting large infrastructure sites in Russia, such as oil refineries and warehouses. But, in his talks with Trump on Tuesday, Zelensky explained the need to hit much smaller and more mobile targets, especially the ballistic-missile batteries that Russian forces have used to hit cities across Ukraine. Last night, as Zelensky and his entourage traveled home through Poland, Russia launched more than 70 missiles, killing at least 10 people in one of the biggest salvos of the war. One of the rockets exploded in Poland.

Starlink offers the most precise means available to steer Ukrainian drones to the Russian missile launchers, many of which are mounted on trucks dispersed across Russia. During his visit to the U.S. this week, Zelensky asked to meet with Musk to talk about his plan for targeting these launchers, but the billionaire declined the invitation, according to one person involved in the discussions. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.

When they met at the White House, Trump told his Ukrainian counterpart that he would consider the requests, but he did not indicate whether he would eventually grant them, one official told told us. Trump did tell Zelensky that he would talk with Musk about it but did not offer a timetable for that conversation or for his eventual decision.

Trump has made no secret of his desire to bring the Russia-Ukraine conflict to a close, and has been frustrated at how long it has taken. One of the officials told us that his eventual decision on Zelensky’s proposal would likely be largely based on whether he felt it could help hasten the end of the conflict. If he thinks that using Starlink would enable Ukraine to push Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table, then Trump may support it. But if he feels it would only escalate matters, then he likely would not, one official told us.

Trump, of course, has been highly deferential to Putin for more than a decade now, and that has hardly changed during this war. Although he has flashed his frustration with the Russian leader at times, he has mostly stayed skeptical of Ukraine’s cause and its chances. But, one official told us, Trump has been impressed with Ukraine’s recent ability to strike deep within Russia with its drone technology and has sensed that Kyiv has some momentum in the conflict (Trump loves to be associated with winners). The meeting remained convivial and Zelensky invoked the memory of the late Senator Lindsey Graham when making his pitch.

With the war in its fifth year, Zelensky emphasized to Trump that Ukraine needs to counter the missile threat before the onset of winter, when Russia may again try to use these weapons to knock out Ukraine’s power grid and heating systems, according to the two officials familiar with the talks.

Without the ability to hit launchers inside Russia, “we have no clear path through this winter,” one of the officials told us. Last winter, Ukraine still had a limited supply of Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and protect its most crucial infrastructure. But the war in Iran has since depleted roughly two-thirds of the U.S. stockpile of these interceptors, according to an analysis published this week by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a research institute based in Washington, D.C. The CSIS report estimated that the U.S. now has as few as 759 of the most advanced Patriot rockets.

Zelensky asked the U.S. to send 300 of these for Ukraine to use this winter. Trump has demurred. Instead, during his talks with Zelensky earlier this month in Ankara, he promised to give Ukraine a license to make its own Patriot interceptors—though Ukraine would not be able to produce them at scale for years.

In the Tuesday meeting, Zelensky argued that Starlink could offer a faster and cheaper answer to the ballistic-missile threat from Russia, according to two of the officials familiar with the conversation. Ukraine already has the long-range drones needed to target missile launchers inside Russia. The Ukrainian company that produces many of them, Fire Point, uses various guidance systems to get around the ban on deploying Starlink inside Russia.

One of the company’s co-founders, Denys Shtilerman, told us that drones equipped with Starlink could prove far more effective than Patriot interceptors in neutralizing the Russian ballistic-missile threat. “Instead of shooting down the arrows, we would strike the archers,” he said.

Inside its own territory, Ukraine has already used Starlink-enabled drones to create what it calls a “kill zone” along the front line—a no-man’s-land, dozens of miles wide, where drones can target any Russian forces that seek to advance. With permission to do the same thing inside Russian territory, “we could widen the kill zone to 500 kilometers,” Shtilerman told us. “If they increase the range of their strikes, we would widen the kill zone all the way to Siberia if needed. The technology would allow us to do that.”

Musk has long resisted the use of Starlink in warfare. The system depends on the world’s largest constellation of satellites to provide a high-speed internet connection to anyone with a Starlink subscription and a receiver. At the start of the Russian invasion, in 2022, Musk provided Ukraine with Starlink receivers free of charge. Ukrainian hospitals, emergency workers, and government agencies used them to stay online despite Russian attacks on the country’s internet infrastructure. The armed forces of Ukraine soon began using Starlink to coordinate troop movements and pilot drones, and the system became the backbone of Ukraine’s military communications.

During some of Ukraine’s most brazen strikes against Russian forces, Musk got cold feet. “How am I in this war?” Walter Isaacson quoted him as asking in his 2023 biography. “Starlink was not meant to be involved in wars. It was so people can watch Netflix and chill and get online for school and do good, peaceful things, not drone strikes.”

That year, the Pentagon began contracting with SpaceX for the communications services it provides to Ukraine’s armed forces. The company also created a separate network, known as Starshield, for use in defense and national security. During his talks with Trump on Tuesday, Zelensky suggested that if Musk refuses to allow the use of Starlink for strikes on Russia, the Pentagon could give Ukraine access to the Starshield network for the same purpose, two of the officials told us.

One of them added, however, that Starshield would not work as well for Ukraine. “It’s more expensive, more complicated, more difficult to integrate into our systems,” the official said. “We have long figured out how to fly drones on Starlink. It would not be hard for us to send them across the border. But Starshield is a somewhat different system. We would need to figure out how to integrate it.” That leaves Starlink as the cheapest and most reliable guidance system available for Ukraine’s long-range drones.

From Musk’s earlier decisions, it can be hard to discern a coherent strategy toward the war in Ukraine. He has used Starlink in ways that each of the warring sides has perceived as helping the other. A few months into the Russian invasion, Musk began to complain about the spiraling cost of providing Ukraine with Starlink service. He refused a Ukrainian request in September 2022 to use Starlink in an attack on Russian warships in Crimea, arguing that the operation risked a nuclear response from the Kremlin.

The following month, Musk published a four-point plan for peace in a post on Twitter. (He would buy the social network for $44 billion a few weeks later.) His peace plan hewed closely to Russian demands, including a provision for Ukraine to remain “neutral” after the war. In response, Zelensky posted his own Twitter survey, asking whether people preferred the Musk who supports Ukraine or the one who supports Russia. Andriy Melnyk, who served as Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany at the time, also shot back at Musk’s peace plan: “Fuck off is my very diplomatic reply to you @elonmusk.”

In Zelensky’s wartime government, the official who cultivated the strongest ties with Musk and SpaceX was Mykhailo Fedorov, the chief architect of the Ukrainian drone program. Early this year, while serving as minister of defense, Fedorov persuaded Musk to shut off the Starlink receivers that Russian forces had been using to fly their own drones in Ukraine. But Fedorov lost his job this month in a government reshuffle, which cost Ukraine its main point of contact with Musk. “Fedorov has a super constructive relationship with him,” a Ukrainian official told us. “So the timing is very bad to install a new minister.”

One person close to Fedorov told us that, in the weeks before he was fired, the minister lobbied Musk and various other contacts in the U.S. to allow the use of Starlink for drone strikes into Russia. Fedorov received assurances from Musk that it would be possible “if Trump says to do it,” the person said. The talks broke off, he added, after the government reshuffle. (Fedorov did not respond to a request for comment.)

The Trump administration could have its own reasons to balk at Zelensky’s request. “It’s one thing to let Ukraine do this on its own territory,” the Ukrainian official said. “It’s another thing to use American technology on the territory of Russia to take out their air defenses, their launchers for ballistic missiles. This is an unfriendly act. I don’t know how Russia could react to that.”

Russia recently deployed new methods for interfering with Starlink signals in Ukraine. Earlier this month, a set of documents was published that appeared to show Russia plotting with China to destroy Starlink satellites, through either hacking, jamming, or knocking them out of orbit. The documents, allegedly produced by China and obtained by The Insider, highlighted the risks Musk faces in helping Ukraine fight the war.

His willingness to broaden that assistance could depend on the leverage Trump has over Musk—and his desire to use it for Ukraine’s benefit. Earlier this month, Trump seemed open to Zelensky’s strategy for pressuring Russia to negotiate a peace deal. “It’s an escalation,” Trump said when asked about Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries and military targets deep inside Russia. Seated beside Zelensky in Ankara, Trump added: “But it’s also an escalation that could help lead to an end.”

entries.title: Abandon Hope, All Ye Who Enter the Mar-a-Lago in Heaven
entries.summary: Tour the mansion in the sky to which Sean Hannity has consigned Lindsey Graham’s soul.
entries.content:
Tour the mansion in the sky to which Sean Hannity has consigned Lindsey Graham’s soul.

Lindsey, Mr. President, I would argue in my mind, probably has a heavenly version of Mar-a-Lago. It may even be a little bigger. He may have a little more gold in the Oval Office in his mansion in heaven, and I wouldn’t be surprised if he added one big, beautiful ballroom and an arch somewhere on the property because he would want to obviously duplicate his dearest friend in life, you, Mr. President.

— Sean Hannity, at Senator Lindsey Graham’s funeral

The Mar-a-Lago in heaven is even bigger than it looks. But it’s less crowded than it might be, considering that it’s the Mar-a-Lago in heaven.

Look at the chip-and-putt golf course! Admire the vista stretching from the sea to the lake. There is croquet. There is European-style terrace dining. And six tennis courts! Or pull back from Mar-a-Lago and observe the Reflecting Pool (perfectly American-flag blue), the arch, the Oval Office. This is it—the perfect way to spend eternity!

It isn’t an insult to consign a soul to Mar-a-Lago for all time. This premier final destination received the “coveted” Six Star Diamond Award for its “leading hospitality” in 2008—a fact that the club’s website still boasts. Just look at the amenities. The food here is the best. The chocolate cake at the Mar-a-Lago in heaven is even better than the one Xi Jinping enjoyed at the Mar-a-Lago on Earth while President Trump talked about bombing Syria. (You can’t drop bombs from here, but there is a button you can press for unlimited Diet Cokes.) Many such treats are available! Enjoy the president’s playlist, the most wonderful playlist in the world: The Phantom of the Opera and “Nessun dorma” and “Tiny Dancer” and “Y.M.C.A.” They never tire of playing “Y.M.C.A.”! It is heaven, after all.

For entertainment, giant TVs play Hannity and Meet the Press, 24/7! Or if you want to read, you’re in luck: There are classified documents too, lying around in cardboard boxes. You can spend forever paging through them if you like. If you get bored of state secrets, visit the ballroom. It is so big and so secure, secure as a fortification. To keep something out? Or to keep something in? No, no one would ever wish to escape this heaven, a heaven interior-decorated according to the wishes of Donald J. Trump. It is good to be here for all eternity.

Sometimes the sky gets very thick with smog, but that is just because they are burning clean coal. No horrible windmills here! Sometimes you hear coughing, but that isn’t your concern. How long has it been since you heard birdsong or genuine, unfeigned laughter? No matter—why don’t you admire the gold finishings? So many gold finishings! Just when you think you are done admiring them, more sprout up! You can also admire the arch, or what you can see of it. It’s huge, too tall for you to make out the top. It seems to pierce through the roof of heaven itself. Looking at it makes you feel dizzy and disoriented, and you start to feel that you cannot tell up from down. Are you looking down from a great height or up at a great height? Where is your compass? You should have packed your compass!

No! It is all right. You are all right. Only a true compass could have steered you to such an exclusive place as this. Mar-a-Lago is heaven, and heaven would be incomplete without Mar-a-Lago. To say so is not to flatter power but to speak from your heart, as Sean Hannity knows. And in heaven a true heart is always rewarded. And so, of course, here you are.

Perfect bliss, after all, to spend eternity haunting another man’s marble halls. Better to reign in hell than serve in heaven? That’s the devil talking! He didn’t know Mar-a-Lago was an option.

entries.title: The Return of ‘Move Fast and Break Things’
entries.summary: The AI industry is getting sloppier.
entries.content:
The AI giants talk a big game about the future they’re building. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has previously written that AI could usher in a world so perfect that “many will be literally moved to tears”—a world pruned of disease, poverty, and illiberalism. “We’re now in the singularity,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said over the weekend on a podcast, and it will be “awesome for the world.” In an interview last week, Elon Musk declared that, in a decade’s time, AI will make us so prosperous that “money won’t matter.”

Unfortunately, life with AI is, so far, less glorious than what’s been promised. The same day that Altman heralded the singularity, Claude users discovered something alarming: Many conversations with Anthropic’s chatbot were available on the open web, discoverable with a Google search. Those public logs and projects reportedly contained medical records, phone numbers, internal corporate documents, and cryptocurrency-wallet keys.

Anthropic was quick to point out that users were responsible for the material being available online: The chatbot gives people the option to “share” their AI conversations via a link that they can send to other people or post online. Claude notes that these links are “public,” which means they can also be hoovered up by Google Search. An Anthropic spokesperson told me that “these shareable links are not guessable or discoverable unless people choose to share them themselves. When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.”

No reasonable person would assume that creating and sharing a link to an AI conversation or presentation would make it searchable by anybody on the World Wide Web. The Claude interface does caution that publishing an “Artifact”—Anthropic’s terms for dashboards and other minor tools made with Claude—could make it “potentially visible in search engine results,” but it does not provide such an explicit warning when sharing a chat. As of this writing, the Claude chat logs no longer appear to be searchable, but at least some Claude Artifacts are.

Those exposed chats were just the latest in a seemingly endless string of AI snafus: misinformation, data leaks, cybersecurity breaches. Immediately after the launch of ChatGPT, one could charitably argue that these lapses were by-products of a new and strange technology. Altman remains fond of saying that the AI industry must learn “from contact with reality.”

But four years into the AI boom, attributing these blunders to growing pains is too convenient. The sheer volume of transgressions—many of them predictable—suggests that what’s actually happening here is widespread carelessness. The same AI executives who promise that their products will deliver human civilization to a triumphant future seemingly cannot release consumer-grade tools without face-planting.

This isn’t Anthropic’s first time leaking user conversations. Last fall, hundreds of Claude chat logs were also inadvertently indexed by Google. At the time, Anthropic attributed the episode to users posting share links online. Last year, OpenAI and xAI exposed hundreds of thousands of conversations in a similar fashion; a number of shared Grok conversations remain searchable. Neither OpenAI nor xAI immediately responded to a request for comment.

Then there are all of the other blunders. Just last week, OpenAI models autonomously hacked into another tech firm, Hugging Face, during internal testing. The issues that led to this sort of attack are fairly well documented, but OpenAI failed to stop its own bots from breaking out. Hugging Face has since said that the OpenAI models appeared to have been rogue for several days. Earlier this week, Reuters reported that OpenAI models had hacked a customer account of yet another tech company.

Altman, Amodei, and many other AI executives have repeatedly warned about AI-enabled cyberattacks and the possibility of models going “rogue.” Meanwhile, their own products are making the entire ecosystem feel more unreliable and dangerous.

It’s easier than ever to launch widespread hacking and phishing campaigns, and AI-written code has itself been shown to have more security flaws than human-written programs. Although AI systems are being tightly woven throughout the infrastructure of the internet, they crash frequently. Hackers recently discovered that a Meta AI customer-service bot would hand over access to tens of thousands of Instagram accounts if asked. (A Meta spokesperson told me that this “wasn’t due to the AI agent itself.”) Nonconsensual porn—that is, sexually explicit material made using the likeness of real people, unbeknownst to them—can be generated with more ease and speed and at greater scale than ever before. And at this point, you can probably assume that most of the text you read on LinkedIn or X is AI-generated.

Despite its grandiose promises, Silicon Valley is embarking upon an era of profound irresponsibility. Last year alone, ChatGPT allegedly pushed people into mental-health spirals, Google Gemini’s under-13 version was easily coaxed to “talk dirty,” and Grok repeatedly spouted racist bile. As quickly as these errors were addressed, new ones cropped up.

Silicon Valley has a long history of world-historic invention and progress—and it also has a long history of impressive rhetoric and disappointing realities. Facebook promised to “bring the world closer together,” Google to “organize the world’s information,” Twitter to foment democracy around the globe. For better or worse, people have experienced dramatic changes as those promises have played out around us almost in real time.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s prophecies are grander and vaguer: Utopia is forever on the horizon, but we don’t have a clear deadline or a road map of how we get there. And apparently, those leading this charge toward the future care little about what happens along the way.

OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Google DeepMind have become behemoths practically overnight. For now, they are growing because of their recklessness, not in spite of it; in the quest to erect a digital god, the internet has become collateral damage. Perhaps these companies really will remake human civilization—but in the meantime, they can’t stop leaking your chats.

entries.title: The White-Collar Myth
entries.summary: Since the 19th century, office jobs have represented a path to comfort and prestige. The AI era is testing whether that promise still holds.
entries.content:
Since the 19th century, office jobs have represented a path to comfort and prestige. The AI era is testing whether that promise still holds.

This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

A New York City ferry terminal in the late 1860s: Commuters issue forth into Lower Manhattan’s maze of streets. They move in distinct waves through the morning. First come the working-class employees in their flannel shirts, off to jobs in factories and shops for little pay. Then around 7 a.m., the crowd shifts, and the clothing with it. “The shirts of the passengers begin to whiten and raiment to improve,” the New-York Tribune reporter and occasional Atlantic contributor Junius Henri Browne observed. These were the office workers—the “salesmen, accountants, clerks, most of whom are young and seem hopeful.” Unlike the manual laborers before them, these men strode confidently into their days, carried forward by visions of partnerships, financial success, and “princely incomes.”

Browne was witnessing the great sartorial and social divide that would define basic American ideas about work and status. Although not a sociologist in any modern sense, he was reckoning with a question that would occupy academics and theorists in the century to come: What separated the hopeful clerks from the mechanics who arrived before them? What did the white shirt, later reduced to just the white collar, signify? As Browne saw, it marked not just a different kind of work but also a different set of expectations. Performing mental rather than manual labor promised comfort, affluence, and status. But he wondered how many people would ever attain the prosperity and standing that they coveted—and whether they were all just feeding themselves on “the sweet fruit” of their “own imagining.”

By the middle of the 20th century, the share of white-collar workers was rapidly overtaking that of blue-collar counterparts. Their affluence shaped consumer society, popular culture, higher education, and a new suburban geography. Questions lingered—were they too comfortable, too conformist, too caught up in their status?—but from some perspectives, they seemed poised to rise even further. Knowledge work, a term first coined in 1959 by the management theorist Peter F. Drucker, described the idea that some white-collar employees’ specialized education and job-related expertise would become prized resources, giving the workers value that companies could not replace—a proposition that he later argued would be cemented by the internet. Now, four years into the age of artificial intelligence, the certainties about office labor are fading, and the questions returning. If knowledge, expertise, and other hallmarks of “brain-work” no longer have the same value, what will remain of the distinctions that once set white-collar workers apart?

In the postwar years, academic studies, magazine articles, novels, and movies puzzled over the new class of office employees. They didn’t own farms, shops, or businesses, but their salaried status distinguished them from hourly wage workers. They relied on employers for their livelihoods yet generally rejected unions and seldom thought of themselves as laborers. Such conditions placed them in an ambiguous place in American society: economically dependent, socially aspirational, neither owners nor willing to identify themselves as ordinary workers. In 1957, an anonymous labor organizer lamented the impossibility of unionizing offices, writing in Harper’s that “the white collar worker is just a different breed.”

What these new conditions of work and status were doing to people’s psychology was an open question. In 1951, the sociologist C. Wright Mills published an anatomy of the “white-collar world” in which he almost pitied his subjects as “cheerful robots” who had traded autonomy for middle-class status. The massive management structures in which they worked provided safety and comfort but made them people pleasers and conformists afflicted by anxiety and emptiness, he argued: The white-collar worker “is always somebody’s man,” a small creature who is acted upon “but does not rise.” He wasn’t alone in his analysis. Six years later, when Charles J. Rolo reviewed a trio of books in this genre for The Atlantic, he asserted that “the daring young man” had been “eclipsed by the earth-bound young man who settles for mediocrity on the installment plan.”

The concept of knowledge work offered another theory of the office that would prove remarkably enduring. Where Mills and other critics had seen dependence and lonely drudgery, Drucker saw the possibility of power for a subset of the white-collar class. “Knowledge workers,” he wrote in The Atlantic in 1994, “will give the emerging knowledge society its character, its leadership, its social profile.” And far from undermining knowledge workers’ status, the internet and the “Information Revolution” would crown it. Writing in the magazine in 1999, Drucker argued that the world taking shape would belong to workers who could synthesize knowledge and analysis. “The key is not electronics,” he explained. “It is cognitive science.” Enhanced by computers, knowledge workers would become so powerful, and so essential, that companies would have to “bribe” them to stay.

Nearly 30 years later, such confidence is in short supply. The advent of a new breed of cheerful robots in the workplace—actual robots; notoriously agreeable—has threatened to disrupt not just the functions of white-collar and knowledge workers, but also their long-standing social markers. Speculation about the implications of AI for white-collar labor abounds. High-school students consider entering the trades over attending university; college students fret over the market for entry-level jobs, while some drop out to vibe code apps. Seasoned workers squint sidelong at AI visionaries’ predictions that they won’t be needed much longer.

Whether AI ultimately destroys office jobs, creates new forms of knowledge work, or does something in between remains impossible to say. What’s clear is that after generations of white-collar work seeming to offer a stable path to status and security, the bargain again feels uncertain. The question that Browne asked on the ferry dock presents itself anew: Who are these people, and where do they think they’re going?

entries.title: The Real Antidepressant Crisis
entries.summary: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. says Americans overuse SSRIs. In fact, too many people who need depression treatment aren’t getting any.
entries.content:
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. says Americans overuse SSRIs. In fact, too many people who need depression treatment aren’t getting any.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is vocal about his view that Americans overuse psychiatric medications, particularly antidepressants. As a general rule, the Health and Human Services secretary is skeptical of pharmaceuticals, but he’s gone further in his critiques of SSRIs, suggesting without credible evidence that their use might be linked to violent behavior, including school shootings. This past spring, he announced plans to discourage doctors from prescribing antidepressants and encourage them to de-prescribe the drugs—that is, to help patients who have previously been prescribed SSRIs stop taking them.

According to a recent survey, about 17 percent of American adults take an antidepressant. Some of them are my patients, many of whom were upset or infuriated by Kennedy’s move to rein in the prescribing of drugs whose benefits they have experienced firsthand. One of my patients, who has tried to stop taking Zoloft several times only for his depression to recur, told me that he couldn’t understand why the nation’s health secretary might want to discourage people from taking the SSRIs they’ve been prescribed.

Kennedy’s claim that antidepressants are overprescribed contains a grain of truth. Some patients receive antidepressants without really needing them or stay on them for longer than necessary. Earlier this year, an independent task force of psychiatrists suggested that more attention be paid to how and when patients and their doctors test whether tapering off these medications would be reasonable. In fact, inappropriate prescribing creates the impression among both patients and doctors that antidepressants are less effective than they are.

When Kennedy talks about de-prescribing antidepressants, exactly what he’s proposing remains unclear. He doesn’t specify which groups of depressed patients he believes can stop their medication. In fact, contrary to his often-heated rhetoric about SSRIs, he said in May when announcing the de-prescription measures that “if you are taking psychiatric medication, we are not telling you to stop”—and then encouraged such patients to “make the right decision” in consultation with their doctor. The benefits of antidepressants vary greatly. There is abundant evidence that antidepressants are effective for people who have moderate or more severe forms of depression. If you feel persistently sad, believe that life isn’t worth living, and lose your energy, appetite, concentration, or ability to experience pleasure, you likely have clinical depression, and your symptoms would be good targets for antidepressant treatment. But the same is not true of people experiencing what psychiatrists call everyday distress. Feeling, say, unhappy in a soul-sucking job or grief-stricken over the loss of a loved one are painful but entirely appropriate emotional responses. They call for changing your situation or contacting a friend for support, not for an antidepressant.

Taking an SSRI in such a scenario would be like prescribing an antibiotic for a common cold: a waste of resources that’s likely to only give the patient side effects and leave them questioning the efficacy of the drug. Some providers nevertheless prescribe antidepressants for everyday distress. I’ve seen patients going through grief or job loss who were prescribed SSRIs by my colleagues, perhaps because they thought the patients were right on the edge of depression. And in the clinic where I teach and supervise residents, I’ve met many people who were unnecessarily prescribed a cocktail of antidepressants by other clinicians in the community. Many of my colleagues have come across such patients too.

Even people who have chronic mild depression can respond well to antidepressants, some studies have found. But a 2010 meta-analysis showed that people with the most severe depression experienced the greatest improvement from antidepressant treatment, whereas the benefit for those with milder depression was smaller, in some cases near zero. One possible explanation for this finding is that placebo responses tend to be higher in patients with milder depression (perhaps because they start to feel better when researchers ask how they’re doing throughout the study), so drug-placebo differences in that group are slight. Another explanation is that people with more severe depression likely have more biological abnormalities in the brain, such as elevated levels of the stress hormone cortisol and exaggerated responses in the fear circuit, which can be good targets for antidepressants.

No national data prove that antidepressant overuse is rampant, though. The closest approximation we have is a landmark 2014 study that examined the health records of more than 1 million patients during one year of treatment and found that about 40 percent of antidepressant prescriptions were written without a documented psychiatric diagnosis. This, however, doesn’t prove that the prescriptions were medically unnecessary: Antidepressants are legitimately prescribed for other reasons, including pain, quitting smoking, and insomnia. And the fact that nearly a fifth of Americans are taking an antidepressant is in line with the actual burden of psychiatric illness in the general population: In the most recent national data available, which were published in 2005, 7 percent of survey respondents reported having major depressive disorder, 4 percent reported PTSD, and others reported additional diagnoses for which SSRIs can be appropriate.

Of course, some patients don’t like being on antidepressants, even if they experience an improvement in their mood. A small proportion of SSRI users experience side effects such as decreased libido, weight gain, and tiredness. Although these effects can understandably be distressing, they are also commonly transient and manageable. If Kennedy’s efforts lead to widespread de-prescribing of antidepressants, it would be a potentially harmful overreaction to a limited problem.

Meanwhile, Kennedy’s focus on antidepressant overprescribing ignores—and may even deepen—a more urgent crisis in psychiatry. The 2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health found that roughly one in three adults who experienced a major depressive episode received no treatment for their illness that year. Evidence suggests that several common barriers drive this undertreatment of depression: People don’t know where to go for help, think they can manage without help, or cannot afford help. In my experience, some depressed patients avoid treatment because they feel that a depression diagnosis is stigmatizing and connotes that they are weak rather than medically ill. The more doubts Kennedy and other officials instill about antidepressants, the more likely some people who really need them may be to turn them down. “The United States is facing a growing challenge of overmedicalization in behavioral health care,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, told The Atlantic in an email. “Under Secretary Kennedy’s leadership, HHS is committed to ensuring that patients and clinicians have transparent information about the benefits, risks, side effects, and potential withdrawal effects of psychiatric medications so they can make informed, evidence-based treatment decisions.”

Depression is a serious illness, and discouraging people who need antidepressants from seeking them—or enacting policies that impede access to them—would only spur on its greatest harms. Roughly half of people who experience an episode of major depression will go on to have a chronic course of the illness. That means many patients cannot stop taking antidepressants without a significant risk of relapse or worse: Depression carries a lifetime suicide risk of about 2 to 9 percent, with more severe forms of the disease corresponding to higher risk. In this sense, depressed patients are dependent on their SSRIs in the same way that people with high blood pressure are dependent on their antihypertensive drugs. To mitigate the risk of fatal complications of the illness, you might have to stay on the treatment for life. That kind of dependency is something that competent clinicians and health-policy experts should encourage.

Kennedy, by contrast, has likened antidepressant dependence to heroin addiction. “Listen, I know people, including members of my family, who’ve had a much worse time getting off of SSRIs than people have getting off heroin,” he told a Senate committee at his confirmation hearing last year. But the fact is that, unlike an opiate such as heroin, antidepressants do not make people high and do not result in habituation, which requires users to take ever-larger doses to maintain their clinical effect. And although research on tapering is somewhat limited, one of the largest available studies shows that any withdrawal symptoms tend to be mild and dissipate within weeks.

Kennedy’s desire to reduce Americans’ reliance on antidepressants fits in with his larger antipathy toward pharmaceuticals, especially vaccines. He generally seems to believe that eating and exercising well is all that is necessary for health. In the case of depression, he favors non-drug alternatives, such as psychotherapy, exercise, and “real food.” But I’ve seen many patients in exemplary physical health—for example, triathletes and serious swimmers who adhere to strict diets—become suicidally depressed. Taking an antidepressant after you have tried exercise, a healthy diet, and psychotherapy isn’t a sign of weakness or a character flaw. It’s a recognition that disease has an underlying biological basis—and that sometimes, you need medication to get better.

entries.title: Dead-Mall Vibes at the Kennedy Center
entries.summary: There’s just one sign of life.
entries.content:
Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency, a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term.

To find any real sign of life at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts these days, you have to trek to the farthest edge of its 17-acre campus.

That’s where I found myself on a pleasant evening last week to catch the only performance scheduled that day at the nation’s once-premier cultural center. Trailing a set of latecomers, I snaked around the center’s facade (where, yes, Kennedy’s name is still tarped), down a path toward the Reach annex, and through its back doors before finally finding the music: a fusion of jazz and R&B drifting from the River Pavilion for dozens of people who filled the indoor-outdoor space. The last time I’d seen a sizable crowd outside the center, hundreds of protesters had amassed while construction workers set up to remove President Trump’s name from the building. And it had been longer, still, since I’d seen a crowd gathered for an actual performance.

As I took in the scene, my phone chimed with a message from a person working inside the main building: a photo capturing the enormous velvet-lined Hall of States, empty of activity. “Here’s the Kennedy Center tonight,” the person wrote. “We’re not doing much.” Other staffers have described the institution to me as a ghost town.

The Kennedy Center once drew some of the world’s most prominent acts, epitomizing Washington’s cosmopolitan ambitions. Since February 2025, however, it has been far better known for institutional turmoil under Trump than for performances taking place inside the complex. That drama culminated this May when a federal judge upended Trump’s efforts to remake the center, ordering the removal of his name and temporarily halting his plans to close the institution for a two-year renovation project that critics call unnecessary. Now, as the center’s leadership reconsiders a path forward, nearly every stage has gone dark for the foreseeable future. No opera (the Washington National Opera severed its affiliation). No musicals (touring shows book schedules months, if not years, ahead of time). No orchestra concerts (the resident symphony has been unable to announce its new season, further imperiling the ensemble’s financial health).

One exception remains. The long-running Millennium Stage has quietly held the line with free weekly events, carrying forward one of the center’s founding ideals: that performing arts should be accessible to everyone. At an institution where nearly everything else has been muted, the most enduring expression of what the Kennedy Center once was now lives on its smallest stage.

That’s by design, according to multiple people familiar with the program’s operations, who spoke with me on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters. The goal is to preserve a sense of continuity—to make it feel as though, despite everything else that’s happened under Trump, there’s still some art at the Kennedy Center. You just have to find the backyard to see it.

When Millennium Stage launched in 1997, Kennedy Center leaders saw it as a way to solve a problem that had dogged the institution since it opened in 1971: Too many people still viewed the nation’s performing-arts center as an intimidating marble monument for just the elite. Millennium Stage offered a different invitation. Each day at 6 p.m., for 365 days a year, anyone could walk in and watch a live performance for free.

The programming spans nearly every artistic discipline—jazz, hip-hop, theater, dance, classical music—and long-standing partnerships with embassies and community organizations helped shape the calendar. “Millennium Stage doesn’t have a genre,” one staffer told me. “It’s something different every day.”

Some of the performances became as exciting as the shows in the center’s main theaters. One evening in 2003, the Colombian singer Juanes drew more than 6,000 fans—mostly of Latin descent, Michael Kaiser, the Kennedy Center’s president from 2001 to 2014, told me. “We were nervous that the fire marshal would shut us down because he was so huge a star, but not quite yet in America,” he said. Other nights featured Earl Scruggs, Patti LaBelle, the National Symphony Orchestra, or performances tied to major international festivals that spilled beyond the Kennedy Center’s ticketed theaters.

Millennium Stage was more than just a free concert series, Kaiser said. It offered tourists another uniquely Washington, D.C., experience after the Smithsonian museums closed for the day. Members of Congress routinely recommended it to constituents visiting Washington. And for many local residents who might never have purchased a ticket to a main-stage production, it became their front door to the institution itself. “I think particularly for those who weren’t going to buy a ticket or couldn’t buy a ticket, this was their link to the Kennedy Center,” Kaiser said.

The recent concert I attended—a performance by the local trumpeter Cyrus “Cy” Mackey and his band, Kenyatta—looked like an effortless, low-lift production. Crews fluidly worked the livestream cameras. A cashier manned a concession stand. Stagehands and security personnel directed guests to open seats. Behind the scenes, though, keeping these shows going requires a small army of planners, producers, and technicians. Artists are booked months in advance. Contracts are negotiated. The stage is configured.

When the Kennedy Center reopened in 2021 after closing during the pandemic, Millenium Stage went down to four concerts a week. Then came the Trump takeover. Under leaders installed by the president, the center saw severe staff layoffs, artist and audience boycotts, and more programming in line with political priorities. Along the way, Millennium Stage absorbed many of the same pressures facing the rest of the institution. Responsibilities that had once been divided among specialists were redistributed among a skeleton crew.

Scroll through the Kennedy Center’s event calendar, and it’s immediately clear how tenuously the institution is hanging on. Aside from Millennium Stage, the only other department producing programming is education, another staffer told me: art-studio sessions geared toward families.

The center hosted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in late June, and its last big productions, Moulin Rouge and Bluey’s Big Play, had their final shows earlier this summer. The main drama has been in court. This week, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper set an August deadline for the Kennedy Center to provide an update on its plans for future construction and operations, as well as the status of the tarp and scaffolding still obscuring the building’s facade. But in the two months since Cooper’s May ruling, Kennedy Center leaders have not moved much closer to offering any clarity about its future. Board members last month voted to appeal Cooper’s ruling but have weighed in on little else so far. The upshot: The Kennedy Center cannot close right now. But it has entered near-stasis, like a dead mall that has just a couple of active storefronts. (An exhibit about President Kennedy is also still open, and volunteers are giving tours.)

Meanwhile, to maintain programming for Millennium Stage, quiet compromises have been made. Earlier this month, the schedule was pared back again—to two or three performances each week, plus a Saturday film screening—and the series moved from its longtime home in the Grand Foyer to the River Pavilion at the Reach, the Kennedy Center’s 2019 expansion along the Potomac River.

By law, the Kennedy Center has to serve as a presidential memorial and present artistic programming—a dual duty that Trump’s surprise plan to close down the center for renovations threatened. Matt Floca, the center’s executive director, testified in April that leaders were exploring options at the Reach so that the Kennedy Center could maintain artistic programming even if the main performance spaces are closed. As the institution’s newest addition, the Reach will likely be the home for any remaining programming this year, one of the staffers I spoke with told me.

Another task for Millennium Stage is rebuilding trust. “The center as a whole has done a lot of damage” to its relationships with artists, another staffer said. Some musicians and agents have quietly asked whether performing at the Kennedy Center is still worth it—or even whether it feels safe.

Notably, Yasmin Williams, an acclaimed fingerstyle guitarist who had been critical of the center’s new leadership, said she was heckled by Trump supporters while performing at Millennium Stage last September. At the time, she told me that she believed the jeering had been a coordinated effort to harass and intimidate her after she obtained an email from a Republican group that had encouraged its members to attend her show to “make sure the audience is filled with patriots!” There have not been any other public reports of politically charged disruptions at Millenium Stage events; a network of previously established relationships with local artists keeps the stage going. Friends recommend friends. Artists reassure other artists. Community, in many ways, has become the infrastructure filling the gaps in a hollowed-out institution.

The other part of Millennium Stage’s resilience is financial. Unlike many of the Kennedy Center’s programs, it is supported by separate endowment funding. As Kennedy Center leaders continue weighing what the institution will look like in the years ahead, the board has yet to settle on a long-term operating plan. But across all of the scenarios being discussed internally, Millennium Stage is widely expected to continue to operate, I was told.

Until then, every Thursday, Friday, and Saturday evening, musicians still tune their instruments and families still wander in. Through it all, Millennium Stage seems to have maintained a core fan group. Mackey, the trumpeter I saw perform, told me he’s grateful the series brings in a diverse crowd. “I saw a lot of youth that were really connecting with the music,” he said. “I saw older ones really connecting with the music—people from different languages, different places.”

One attendee I spoke with after the show said he has been joining his friends and family for concerts every summer in the past few years. “Usually, we get together by the harbor,” Daniel Mariam told me as he sat in a lawn chair outside the pavilion—though sometimes, like on this night, he said, he is the only one from his group who shows up. “Every time there is a concert, I’m here.”

entries.title: Trump Is Barely Pretending About Comey Anymore
entries.summary: The vindictive and meritless plot against the former FBI director is being orchestrated almost entirely in public view.
entries.content:
The vindictive and meritless plot against the former FBI director is being orchestrated almost entirely in public view.

Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency, a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term.

Legal filings submitted by James Comey this week argue that the Trump administration has subjected the former FBI director to a vindictive and meritless prosecution. What stands out is how little effort the president put into pretending this is not the case.

President Trump first branded Comey a criminal more than eight years ago. In 2017, he took the then-shocking step of firing Comey before the expiration of his 10-year term. The following year, Trump wrote a Twitter post claiming, “James Comey is a proven LEAKER & LIAR. Virtually everyone in Washington thought he should be fired for the terrible job he did—until he was, in fact, fired. He leaked CLASSIFIED information, for which he should be prosecuted.”

Hampered by career public servants and political appointees who followed traditional democratic norms (refusing to prosecute people merely because the president hates them), Trump was unable to make good on this threat and settled mostly for tweeting out demands that Comey be imprisoned. During his second term, however, Trump has sought to bring criminal charges against apparently anybody who defies or displeases him. He has flexed this power by repeating his claims that Comey was a “dirty cop” who deserved prison, ordering the Justice Department to charge him with crimes, and orchestrating the entire plot in public view.

Last year, Trump reportedly pressured the Justice Department to charge Comey. When the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, Erik Siebert, resigned rather than bring a meritless case, Trump’s Justice Department replaced him with Lindsey Halligan, an inexperienced Trump loyalist, who brought an indictment for lying to Congress (an allegation that was different from his first-term claims that Comey had leaked classified material). It was shortly dismissed when a judge found that Halligan had been unlawfully appointed.

Trump ordered Attorney General Pam Bondi to bring new charges and fired her for, among other reasons, failing to accomplish the task. He then replaced Bondi with another loyalist, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who duly produced another indictment, this time for the “crime” of threatening the president’s life by posting an Instagram photo of seashells on the beach spelling out “86 47.” Trump showed Blanche the man, and Blanche found the crime.

When Comey’s message appeared, Trump’s supporters depicted it as an endorsement of his murder, rather than his removal. Comey immediately removed the post and clarified his intentions, stating he opposed political violence. Trump has nevertheless insisted that “86,” a restaurant shorthand for canceling an order or ejecting a customer that has taken on a general meaning “to get rid of or discard,” must imply a call for presidential assassination.

Even if this implausible interpretation were correct, Comey’s message would not be a crime. Under the Supreme Court’s long-standing interpretation of the First Amendment, advocating violence against a public official, though morally reprehensible, is protected speech, as long as it does not constitute a specific incitement to immediate action. That is one reason that Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech urging an angry and armed crowd to “fight like hell” to overturn the election result could not be prosecuted.

The current charge against Comey, in short, relies on a tendentious interpretation of an innocuous term combined with a disregard for the First Amendment in order to gin up charges against a man Trump has been targeting openly for nearly a decade.

Although Trump has done little to disguise his intentions, it would be untrue to say he put zero effort into the pretense. He did attempt to keep one of his instructions to Bondi private—a September 20, 2025, message on Truth Social to his then–attorney general stating, “Pam: I have reviewed over 30 statements and posts saying that, essentially, ‘same old story as last time, all talk, no action. Nothing is being done. What about Comey, Adam ‘Shifty’ Schiff, Leticia??? They’re all guilty as hell, but nothing is going to be done,’” and concluding, “We can’t delay any longer, it’s killing our reputation and credibility. They impeached me twice, and indicted me (5 times!), OVER NOTHING. JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!!”

However, Trump mistakenly posted this direct message to his public account, making it visible to all of his followers.

Trump’s incompetence throughout this vendetta against Comey is perhaps its most welcome aspect. The episode reveals the formidable powers available to a president to target his enemies. Comey’s filing alleges that, in addition to Trump’s previously known directives to the Justice Department to prosecute his target, the president used the Secret Service to investigate him.

The agency, which is charged with protecting the president, not only began following Comey, but tracked his location through his phone. This step legally requires law enforcement to believe there is “an imminent threat to life or limb,” which Comey’s retracted seashell message obviously did not constitute.

One Secret Service official wrote in a memo, MS NOW reports, “At the time we did not believe anyone’s life was in danger and legally it was a bad idea.” But after a top Justice Department official demanded this action, the Secret Service relented. The difference between security agencies in democracies and secret-police forces is that the former have to obey laws and not just follow the whims of the head of state. The Secret Service’s actual procedures turn out to be more like guidelines that can be discarded if the president is sufficiently angry—which, from the standpoint of safeguarding democracy, constitutes a fairly concerning loophole.

Not for the first time, the president’s clumsiness is likely to negate his malevolence, though not without considerable cost, in time and money, to Comey. Yet Trump’s incompetence is also unsettling. This president may be succeeded by someone who equals Trump in his eagerness to wield the office’s powers and in his lack of scruples, but exceeds him in intelligence and discipline. Future plots to imprison a critic of the MAGA movement might not be undermined by a loudmouth president who can’t help but give away the scheme.

entries.title: Spider-Man Forgets Itself
entries.summary: Despite seeming like a fresh start, Brand New Day is trapped in the Marvel vortex.
entries.content:
Despite seeming like a fresh start, Brand New Day is trapped in the Marvel vortex.

The subtitle of the newest Spider-Man movie, Brand New Day, implies a grand reset. Yes, this is the fourth Spider-Man installment starring Tom Holland as the spindly hero, not including the other Marvel projects he’s popped in for. This sequel, however, purports to bring the character back to basics, offering a street-level adventure after far too many big crossovers. Its predecessor, No Way Home, mixed up good and bad guys from three different iterations of the Spider-Man franchise for a ridiculous phantasmagoria of clanging action figures. But it ended with a magic spell that made Spider-Man’s true identity (as Peter Parker) unknown to all, even his loved ones; instead, he became an anonymous, local do-gooder battling bank robbers and costumed thugs around New York City. And Brand New Day pretends to tell that story, for about 20 minutes.

The simple, rather depressing, and completely overwhelming fact of the matter is that the Marvel Cinematic Universe cannot be ignored, even as superhero fatigue has definitively set in at the global box office. Spider-Man: Brand New Day briefly aspires to be unconcerned with the plotty goings-on of the Avengers and their ilk, yet as Destin Daniel Cretton’s movie drags on, it’s used as a launchpad for future projects. That Marvel is relying on its best-loved hero—who consistently attracts wide swaths of moviegoers to theaters—to spark some later success makes sense; the approach used to work very well for the MCU. But it has become progressively more exhausting for viewers. Worse still, the sections of Brand New Day that do focus on Spider-Man are maudlin—they dial up his loneliness and malaise while forgetting about the screwball joie de vivre that often sets him apart from the rest of the Marvel catalog.

That tendency toward downbeat storytelling has befallen many Spider-Man films over the years. The character, created by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko, is fundamentally unlucky—repeatedly besieged by public scorn, or money troubles, or romantic turmoil—but he bears that misfortune with spirit and grace; he gleefully swings via web across skyscrapers while the city tosses problem after problem at him. In Brand New Day, though, Peter Parker has become a workaholic. He dons the Spider-Man costume to beat up bad guys, seemingly because he has no social life or family at home.

Peter’s beloved Aunt May (played by Marisa Tomei) died in No Way Home, and his girlfriend, MJ (Zendaya), and best pal, Ned (Jacob Batalon), had their memories of him wiped away for their own protection. Brand New Day’s script, by Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, emphasizes Peter’s growing sense of alienation by having him go through a spider puberty of sorts: He begins to spurt uncontrollable web-fluid from his wrists and experiences total sensory overload every time he goes outside. The idea that Spider-Man is becoming a little too much of an arachnid at the cost of his own humanity could be a fun one, with a nice dollop of body horror. Instead, it mostly involves Peter gloomily walking the streets, gazing at MJ from afar, and then getting sucked into various MCU quests that are hard to feel too invested in.

That includes some business with the Punisher (Jon Bernthal), a hardened antiheroic assassin who has been softened for Brand New Day’s PG-13 environs. Now he’s an outer-borough crank who lives in a tugboat and barks at Spider-Man to stop being such a softie. Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo), a.k.a. the Hulk, makes an appearance, helping Peter puzzle out the scientific mysteries of his ongoing transformation. Then there’s the new, mysterious character played by Sadie Sink, introducing a major element of MCU lore that has very little to do with Spider-Man. I won’t reveal the details for the spoiler-phobic, but it’s dispiriting that Sink’s entire storyline not only feels forced in but also seems desperately cribbed from Stranger Things, the show on which the actor first made an impression.

For much of the baggy running time, Spider-Man is less of a likable urban superhero and more a friendly neighborhood bystander. Holland’s performance in this role has always been winning; he has a Marty McFly–esque chirpiness that suits Peter’s inherent nerdiness, and he’s just as capable of delivering a puppy-dog stare as befits the big, broad emotions of comic-book storytelling. Despite numerous outings, however, Holland’s Spider-Man has never really gotten the chance to save the day on his own. His entries have always been besieged by cameos from popular characters such as Iron Man, Nick Fury, or, as in No Way Home, the Spider-Men that preceded Holland’s take. Brand New Day opens with a montage of Spider-Man duking it out with villains solo in New York, yet it feels almost meant to be skipped past.

A prior Marvel film, last year’s The Fantastic Four: First Steps, made that same mistake. It, too, kicked off with a sequence for the fans, showing some favorite comic-book heroes and villains getting quickly dispatched before the actual story revved up. In both cases, the assumption is the same—that theatergoers aren’t there for traditional superhero derring-do, only a cavalcade of Easter eggs and teases for upcoming installments to keep the Marvel gravy train running at full steam. No doubt Brand New Day will make billions and prove that strategy somewhat correct. But for a genuine fan of the kind of throwback these movies could offer, it might be somewhat sad to behold.

entries.title: Is She the New Britney Spears—Or the New Lou Reed?
entries.summary: Charli XCX’s new album is a broadside against overthinking the artistic process.
entries.content:
Charli XCX’s new album is a broadside against overthinking the artistic process.

Earlier this year, I wrote an article with the headline “Slow Down, Charli XCX.” The pop singer had followed a hit album, 2024’s Brat, with a steady pulse of output—a remix album, a soundtrack album, a host of movie roles, plus many, many marketing stunts—that had me exhausted by someone whom I consider to be one of the most exciting voices in music. Quantity was beating quality; good enough was smushing great.

Five months later, a new Charli XCX album has arrived, with all of the memes and metacommentary that tend to swirl around music’s most online star. It’s called Music, Fashion, Film, and it was conceived in what she’s described as a burst of inspiration during last fall’s Paris Fashion Week. With a spiky and Scotch-taped sound, the album is a 30-minute broadside against overthinking the artistic process. In direct challenge to those who feel she’s saturated the market (I’m not the only one), she’s rallying for an idea that feels very now but really is also very old: More is more.

Love songs to the muse abound. “Yeah, we’re so inspired / basically all the time,” she sings on the opener, titled “Rock Music,” whose glitch-kissed analog instrumentation and lyrical logorrhea announce the album’s sound and attitude. “Camera” celebrates the sheer terror of acting by comparing the director’s lens to a gun; “Magic Metal Montana” narrates recording-studio-forged friendship while cutesy New Wave riffs percolate. The album closes with a monologue from the director David Cronenberg, who preaches that long-term legacy really can’t be the artist’s concern. His implication is that what matters is what you do in this lifetime—so get to doing it.

Charli is known for making self-aware, cybernetic dance pop—the art-school take on Britney Spears—but this album most flagrantly calls back to a rock band: the Velvet Underground. Lou Reed modeled the sort of petulant sing-talking that characterizes her verses. The album’s producers, A. G. Cook and Finn Keane, have made a digital drag-and-drop collage of the Velvets’ ingredients: tinny guitars evoking 1970’s radio-rock foray, Loaded; metronomic beats in the lineage of the band’s sparse and steady timekeeper, Moe Tucker. Sitting next to Martin Scorsese and the designer Marc Jacobs on the album cover is the group’s multi-instrumentalist John Cale, rock’s god of noisy, dignified experimentation.

Comparisons to the Velvet Underground recontextualize Charli’s career in a useful way. By courting the charts while pulling from the avant-garde, she’s long been at the center of the tiresome debate over “poptimism,” an alleged cultural turn toward valuing easy gratification over difficulty in art. But the Velvets were sneering at the false dichotomy between those things back in the ’60s. Yes, Cale droned with dread, and Reed sang of scandalous topics (I wish Charli and other leading songwriters of her generation held his social-documentarian instincts—rather than fixating on the person in the mirror). But Reed was also a bubblegum fan who sought hits. He shared the ambition Charli sings about on the sterling Music, Fashion, Film B-side “Playboy Bunny”: to make a song as memorable as the canonical smut mag’s logo.

A few tracks here might indeed rate as future classics. With serene guitars and unnervingly beautiful vocals referencing the malaise of doomscrolling, “SS26” glides from the speakers like some chiffon-clad horseman of the apocalypse (“Spring, summer ’26 / When the world is gonna end, no hope for any of it”). The sludgy, distorted “Card Declined” well captures the existential futility of a shopping binge. “Yeah” is a brilliantly simple distillation of the creative process in which Charli mumbles “I don’t wanna” a bunch—until she changes her mind. Surf-rock riffs, punctuated with pockets of silence, eventually slacken in tempo for a glorious, slo-mo finish. The track has a complete thesis about the ups and downs of art making, articulated almost entirely in sound.

Generally, the more words in a song here, the worse it is. Charli’s aiming for sprezzatura, but of course that’s not something you can aim for—and many of the results feel like careless rambling. On the otherwise-delightful, fuzzed-out “Wink Wink,” a line in the first verse is as unpleasant as gristly steak: “And maybe I fucked your dad / Just kidding, I’m only saying that for effect.” Meanwhile, the sweetly nostalgic “2007” is slightly undercooked: “All from your apartment, you can shine bright like”—and here the brain craves some twist—“a star.” The most personal tracks on the album are convoluted yet bland, like the recounting of uninteresting dreams. “Magic Metal Montana” salutes her producer Cook, but her descriptions are superficial—as if Charli doesn’t really know him.

With their unusual production style and intriguing subject matter, many of these songs point to far better versions of themselves. Is it churlish to ask for more oomph, more insight, more effort? The album’s cover seems to answer that question by featuring three masters of modern media who are known for being prolific. Jacobs used to put out 16 fashion lines a year. Scorsese’s all-over-the-place 1980s output was criticized as inconsistent at the time, but fans have come to appreciate The King of Comedy and After Hours. Cale will always be thought of as a genius even if few listened to, say, 2024’s Poptical Illusion. These men create simply because creating is what they do—and audiences have been lucky that’s so.

Charli has every right to take heed from that model. But the artists she’s channeling are icons of a 20th-century paradigm now destroyed by overproduction. After the internet made creation, distribution, and consumption of media into frictionless affairs, pop culture seemed to become swamped: so much content, so few classics. Cronenberg is right that artists need not create with posterity in mind, but for a contemporary oracle such as Charli, the concerns of the present do merit consideration. And the great concern, right now, is too much mediocrity.
